desc:
The pattern p contains lowercase letters, ? (matches exactly one arbitrary letter) and * (matches any sequence of letters, including the empty one). You may edit the string s with single-letter operations, each costing 1: insert a letter anywhere, delete a letter, or replace a letter by another one.

Return the minimum number of edits after which the edited string matches the whole pattern. Pattern characters are never edited.

s = "abc", p = "a*c"   ->  0
s = "abc", p = "a?"    ->  1   (delete c; the ? takes b)
s = "",    p = "a?*"   ->  2   (insert a, then any letter for ?; the star is empty)
s = "xyz", p = "abc"   ->  3
s = "abcd", p = "b*"   ->  1   (replace or delete the first letter)
constraints: s contains only lowercase letters; p contains lowercase letters, ? and *
hints: Combine the ideas of edit distance and of wildcard matching: a table over prefixes of s and prefixes of p whose cells hold a minimum number of edits instead of a boolean.

Let F[i][j] be the fewest edits making s[:i] match p[:j]. A pattern letter can be aligned with s[i-1] (cost 0 if equal, else 1), or s[i-1] can be deleted (+1), or the letter can be inserted (+1). A ? aligns with any letter at cost 0.
A star is free: it can be empty (F[i][j-1]) or swallow one more letter of s (F[i-1][j]). Base: F[i][0] = i; F[0][j] is the number of non-star characters in p[:j].
editorial: Think of an alignment between s and the pattern. Each pattern character is either aligned with one character of s or has no partner (it must then be produced by an insertion, except a star which simply stays empty). Each character of s is either aligned, deleted, or swallowed by a star. This is the edit distance alignment with wildcard-specific costs: a literal aligned with a different letter costs 1 (replace), a literal with no partner costs 1 (insert), a ? aligned with anything costs 0, a ? without partner costs 1 (insert an arbitrary letter), and a star costs 0 however many letters it swallows.

That gives F[i][j] for a literal c = p[j-1] as min(F[i-1][j-1] + (s[i-1] != c), F[i-1][j] + 1, F[i][j-1] + 1); for ? the first term has no mismatch cost; for * it is min(F[i][j-1], F[i-1][j]). Deleting a letter next to a star is never better than letting the star swallow it, so the star rule needs no extra +1. The base values are F[i][0] = i (delete everything) and F[0][j] = F[0][j-1] + (0 if p[j-1] is a star else 1). Time and space are linear in the table size, and a rolling row brings the memory down to O(n).
